content: It is not mandatory to complete all five components of the Annual Patient Monitoring Review (APMR) during every visit. Depending on the specific needs of the facility, one or more activities may be conducted in a single visit. For instance, if a facility lacks adequate patient monitoring tools or if the staff is not sufficiently trained, components two through five may not need to be performed. In such cases, the initial focus should be on providing patient cards and registers, training staff on their use, and emphasizing the importance of patient monitoring tools to ensure continuity of care and effective patient tracking. The five components of an APMR include: 1. A rapid assessment of the patient monitoring system to identify gaps and areas for improvement. 2. Verification of data quality and tallying of key additional indicators from a sample or census of HIV patient cards. 3. Verification of data quality and tallying of key additional indicators from the ART (antiretroviral therapy) register. 4. Completion or verification of the ART cohort report. 5. Validation of the cross-sectional report. The APMR process is instrumental in identifying and understanding gaps in the functionality of the patient monitoring system, data quality, and data aggregation. It also helps in using data to improve the quality of care and in developing action plans to address identified problems. The APMR should be a routine and integral part of the healthcare system. Ensuring data quality and assessing and improving patient care should be regularly performed by the clinical team and district program management team as part of healthcare delivery. Ideally, the APMR should involve collaboration between the facility’s clinical team, district teams (e.g., HIV, TB/HIV, MNCH, and health information staff), technical staff from partner organizations, and regional program staff. The methodology for APMR has been field-tested in countries such as Guyana, Ethiopia, and Namibia. Results indicate that rapid assessments of patient monitoring systems are crucial for identifying gaps and improving overall functionality. Register tallies can be completed at a rate of approximately 100 patients per hour, while card tallies can be done at a rate of 100–150 cards per day, depending on how the cards are filed. Establishing the active patient population from registers takes about 30 minutes per register. Supervisors and data clerks agree that integrating these activities into routine processes is beneficial. Before conducting a rapid assessment of the patient monitoring system, the team should ensure they have received all necessary reports from the facility. Assessment teams should review facility data beforehand to identify potential issues and solutions, allowing for a more focused and constructive use of time. Regular assessments enable the team to concentrate on specific challenges during each visit and track improvements made since the last visit. A checklist should be used to evaluate the integration of HIV, MNCH, and TB patient monitoring systems, assess the functionality of the system, determine the quality and completeness of the data, evaluate human resource capacity and training needs, and formulate an action plan to address identified problems. Data quality is critical for effective patient care and program management. Incomplete, illegible, or misplaced records hinder clinicians’ ability to manage patients and improve programs. Data quality can be enhanced through careful recording and transcription of information. However, since errors are inevitable, data quality assessments should be integrated into periodic reviews or APMRs and conducted routinely. Common data quality issues include incomplete or incorrect entries, such as recording percentages instead of numbers. Key principles for ensuring good data quality include simplifying and standardizing data collection tools, integrating data quality checks into daily practice, and training staff involved in data entry and reporting. Routine reviews of patient records should be conducted to ensure all information is complete, legible, and accurate. Data clerks or other staff responsible for transcribing information should note any incomplete, missing, or implausible data so that issues can be resolved. Allocating time for clerks to provide feedback to clinicians and clarify queries can improve clinical record-keeping. Patient registration and subsequent clinical visits provide opportunities to verify and update demographic data, such as addresses and phone numbers, which are essential for tracing patients who miss appointments. Periodic reviews of patient records, such as during supervision visits or annual monitoring reviews, can help identify data quality issues. For example, supervisors could randomly select 10 patient records and compare the data against the ART register. Comparing data collected at different time points can also help assess data quality. Ideally, data quality should improve over time, but an increasing number of patients on ART may strain the data collection system. Declining data quality makes it difficult to analyze trends. Cohort reports are useful for identifying changes in trends, such as increases in loss to follow-up (LTF) or decreases in the proportion of patients with viral load measurements. To tally key additional data from HIV patient cards, the eligible patient population should first be identified, limited to those seen during the last calendar year. The sample size should then be determined using a standardized methodology, and a sampling interval should be established by dividing the total number of eligible patients by the required sample size. Systematic sampling can then be conducted by marking every Xth patient in the ART register until the sample size is reached. Data should be collected according to indicator instructions, and missing data should be noted to facilitate interpretation and follow-up. Verifying data quality in ART registers involves comparing patient records with register data to ensure consistency. Depending on patient volume, completing paper-based ART registers can be time-consuming. To ensure good-quality data, only collect information that is useful for health facility workers and program managers. Registers should ideally be updated daily or weekly, and electronic registers should allow for real-time data entry. If there is a backlog of patient cards to be entered into the ART register, systematic approaches should be used to address it. This may involve setting aside dedicated days for data entry or concurrently addressing the backlog while entering new patients. Avoiding backlogs is essential, as they can lead to inaccurate data entry and require significant time and effort to resolve.
